meta.subject: science
meta.title: Force, Motion & Work Done
meta.summary: Scalars vs vectors, distance vs displacement, speed and velocity, acceleration and work, in four hands-on labs.

chunks.title: Two kinds of quantities
body: Some things only need a size: **5 kg**, **10 s**, **30 °C**. These are **scalars**.
Others also need a **direction**: **20 N to the left**, **5 m/s East**. These are **vectors**.
This chapter is about that difference, and about what forces do to things.

chunks.title: Lab 1 · The Neighborhood Grid Runner
intro: Walk from the 🏠 to the 🏪. Each square is a 10 m block.
**Green** adds up every step: that's **distance**. **Indigo** points straight from home to you: that's **displacement**.

challenges.text: **Mission:** walk **80 m** of distance but end with **0 m** of displacement.
challenges.explain: You walked 80 m but ended back home, so the arrow from start to finish is 0 m.

challenges.text: **Mission:** reach the shop using the shortest walk possible, **120 m**.

tasks: Take a long, winding route to the shop. Which number keeps growing, and which one ends up the same?

chunks.title: Mini-game · Scalar or vector?
chunks.intro: Drop each quantity into the bucket that matches the question it answers.

challenges.explain: Scalars only need a size. Vectors also need a direction.

question.prompt: You walk 30 m East, then 30 m West. What is your **displacement**?

options.why: 60 m is the **distance**: every step added up. Displacement only compares where you started and where you ended.
That was true halfway. Then you walked back, so you ended where you started.
You never got further than 30 m from the start, and you ended right back at it.

question.explanation: You're back at the start, so the straight-line arrow from start to finish has length **0 m**.

chunks.title: Speed, velocity and acceleration
body: **Speed** is how fast: $5\text{ m/s}$. It's a scalar.
**Velocity** is speed + direction: $+5\text{ m/s}$ (East) or $-5\text{ m/s}$ (West). It's a vector.
**Acceleration** is how much the velocity changes **every second**.

chunks.title: Speed and velocity
chunks.caption: Both are measured in metres per second, $\text{m/s}$.

question.prompt: A runner covers $100\text{ m}$ in $20\text{ s}$. Speed = ___ $\text{m/s}$

mistakes.why: You multiplied. Speed is distance **÷** time: $100 \div 20$.
That's time ÷ distance. Speed is distance ÷ time: $100 \div 20$.

chunks.title: Lab 2 · The Nitro Skateboard Track
intro: Tap the skater to roll. Change the acceleration $a$ while it rolls!
A dot drops every second. Wider gaps mean the skater is going faster.

challenges.text: **Mission:** start from rest ($u = 0$) and cross the finish line in **under 8 s**.
challenges.explain: A big acceleration adds lots of speed every second, so the 90 m flies by.

challenges.text: **Mission:** make the skater **turn around**: start moving East, end up moving West.

tasks: Set $u = 6$ and $a = 0$. What happens to the gaps between the dots, and to the speed?

chunks.title: Acceleration

items.label: unit: metres per second, every second

chunks.caption: $u$ = starting velocity, $v$ = final velocity, $t$ = time. A negative $a$ means slowing down (**deceleration**).

question.prompt: A skater speeds up from $3\text{ m/s}$ to $9\text{ m/s}$ in $2\text{ s}$. Acceleration $a = $ ___ $\text{m/s}^2$

mistakes.why: $9 - 3 = 6$ is the change in velocity. Acceleration is the change **per second**, so divide by $2\text{ s}$.
That's $6 \times 2$. Divide by the time instead of multiplying.

chunks.title: Forces
body: A **force** is a push or a pull. It's measured in **newtons** ($\text{N}$).
Force is a vector: the arrow's **length** shows how strong it is, and its **direction** shows which way.
When several forces act at once, what matters is the **net force**: what's left after they cancel out.

chunks.title: Lab 3 · Tug-of-War & Crate Pusher
intro: Tap **+50** or **+100** to add pullers, then tap the crate to pull!
**Amber** arrows are the pulls, **rose** is friction, **indigo** is the net force.

challenges.text: **Mission:** balance the tug-of-war with **at least 4 people** pulling ($F_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ N}$).
challenges.explain: Equal pulls cancel out: $F_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ N}$, so the crate doesn't speed up.

challenges.text: **Mission:** on the **rough road**, pull hard enough to get the crate moving.

tasks: On **wood**, make the net force $50\text{ N}$. Why doesn't the crate move?

chunks.title: Balanced or unbalanced?
body: **Balanced** forces cancel out: $F_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ N}$, so the object stays as it is.
**Unbalanced** forces: the object moves toward the stronger side.

question.prompt: Two teams pull a rope: $300\text{ N}$ to the right and $300\text{ N}$ to the left. What happens?

options.text: The forces are balanced, so it doesn't speed up

options.why: The right pull is cancelled exactly by the left pull: $300 - 300 = 0\text{ N}$.
Neither side is stronger. $F_{\text{net}} = 0\text{ N}$, so there's no acceleration.

options.text: It gets pulled in both directions at once and speeds up
options.why: Forces in opposite directions **cancel**. The net force decides the motion, and here it's 0 N.

chunks.title: Work done
body: In everyday talk, *work* means getting tired. In science, **work is done only when a force moves something**.
The distance $d$ must be in the **same direction** as the force. Work is measured in **joules** ($\text{J}$).

chunks.title: Lab 4 · The Scientific Work Detector
chunks.intro: Pick a scenario, then tap the picture and watch the **Work Done meter**.

challenges.text: **Mission:** do exactly $1000\text{ J}$ of work on the cart.
challenges.explain: Force × distance = 1000 J, for example $100\text{ N} \times 10\text{ m}$.

challenges.text: **Mission:** push the brick wall with $500\text{ N}$ and check the meter.
**Mission:** carry the bag at least $20\text{ m}$ and read the work done against gravity.

chunks.title: No movement in the force's direction, no work
body: Pushing a wall: huge force, but $d = 0\text{ m}$, so $W = 0\text{ J}$.
Carrying a bag sideways: your force is up, the motion is sideways (90°), so no work is done against gravity.

question.prompt: Ram pushes a box with $20\text{ N}$ across $6\text{ m}$. Work done = ___ $\text{J}$

mistakes.why: You added. Work is force **times** distance: $20 \times 6$.
You divided. Work is force **times** distance: $20 \times 6$.

flashcards.back:
Has size only. *How much?*
Mass, time, speed, distance, temperature

Has size **and** direction. *How much + which way?*
Force, velocity, acceleration, displacement

Distance: the whole path walked (scalar).
Displacement: straight line from start to finish, with a direction (vector).

Speed: how fast ($5\text{ m/s}$).
Velocity: how fast + which way ($-5\text{ m/s}$ = West).

newton, $\text{N}$
The unit of force (a push or a pull).

$W = F \times d$, in joules ($\text{J}$)
Only counts movement in the direction of the force.

questions.prompt: A cyclist speeds up from $2\text{ m/s}$ to $12\text{ m/s}$ in $5\text{ s}$. Acceleration = ___ $\text{m/s}^2$

mistakes.why: $12 - 2 = 10$ is the change in velocity. Acceleration is the change **per second**: divide by $5\text{ s}$.
$(12 + 2) \div 5$ adds the velocities. Use the **difference**: $v - u$.
You multiplied by the time. Divide instead: $10 \div 5$.

hints: Acceleration is how much the velocity changes **each second**.

questions.prompt: A car slows down from $20\text{ m/s}$ to $5\text{ m/s}$ in $3\text{ s}$. Acceleration = ___ $\text{m/s}^2$

mistakes.why: Right size, wrong sign! The car is **slowing down**, so $v - u = 5 - 20$ is negative.
$(20 + 5) \div 3$ adds the velocities. Use the difference $v - u$.
That's the change in velocity. Now divide it by the time, $3\text{ s}$.

hints: Is the car speeding up or slowing down? That tells you the sign.

questions.prompt: You push a box with a force of $50\text{ N}$ and it moves $4\text{ m}$ forward. Work done = ___ $\text{J}$

mistakes.why: You added. Work is force **times** distance.
You divided. Work is force **times** distance.

hints: Did the box move in the direction you pushed? Then work was done.
$W = F \times d$ with $F = 50\text{ N}$ and $d = 4\text{ m}$.

questions.prompt: Sita pushes a wall with $300\text{ N}$ for 2 minutes and gets exhausted. How much work does she do on the wall?

options.why: $300 \times 2$ uses the **time**. $W = F \times d$ uses distance, and the wall moved $0\text{ m}$.
$300 \times 120\text{ s}$ still uses time, not distance. The wall didn't move, so $d = 0$.
That's only the force. Work also needs a distance moved, and here $d = 0\text{ m}$.

hints: Getting tired isn't the same as doing work in science. What does work need?
$W = F \times d$. How far did the wall move?
questions.explanation: The wall didn't move, so $W = 300 \times 0 = 0\text{ J}$.

questions.prompt: A runner does one full lap of a $400\text{ m}$ track and stops exactly where she started. What are her distance and displacement?

options.why: These are swapped. Distance counts the whole path (400 m); displacement is start → finish, which is the same spot.
Displacement is the straight line from start to finish. She finished where she started, so it's 0 m.
Distance counts **every** metre she ran: the whole lap is 400 m.

hints: Distance is a scalar (the whole path). Displacement is a vector (start → finish).
Where did she start, and where did she finish?
Path = 400 m, so distance = 400 m. Start and finish are the same point, so displacement = 0 m.
questions.explanation: Distance = 400 m (the whole lap). Displacement = 0 m (same start and finish).

questions.prompt: A bus travels $120\text{ m}$ in $10\text{ s}$. Its speed is ___ $\text{m/s}$

mistakes.why: You multiplied. Speed is distance **÷** time.
That's time ÷ distance. Divide the distance by the time: $120 \div 10$.

hints: Which formula links speed, distance and time?

rows: One 400 m lap: distance 400 m, displacement 0 m
20 N to the right; 2 m/s² forwards

items.title: Acceleration
items.body: $u$ start velocity, $v$ final velocity, $t$ time. Negative $a$ = slowing down. Unit: $\text{m/s}^2$.

items.title: Net force
items.body: Balanced ($0\text{ N}$): stays as it is. Unbalanced: moves toward the stronger side. Friction opposes motion.

items.title: Speed triangle
items.body: Cover what you want: $d = v \times t$, $t = \tfrac{d}{v}$.

items.title: Work triangle
items.body: $d$ must be along the force. No movement → $0\text{ J}$.
